summary.text:
Two things stand out, and the first is structural. Winchester's day-to-day treasury has been run by Hampshire County Council's Investments and Borrowing Team since September 2014 under a formal joint-discharge arrangement, with Winchester keeping the accounting and all long-term borrowing decisions. The report considers bringing it in-house and rejects that for resilience and economies of scale. It is the only shared treasury service in the library.

The second is Table 5. Bail-in exposure of 100% against 58% for similar authorities, and a weighted average maturity of one day against 45 for peers — the most liquid and most bail-in-exposed portfolio we have priced, and a deliberate consequence of holding short-term unsecured deposits and money market funds. The return, 3.72%, is below both peer groups.

Everything they owe — all £159.3m — is HRA debt including the 2012 settlement, at 3.06% over 17.8 years. Internal borrowing is £118.8m and every table foots.

The live item is forward: the liability benchmark reaches £201.1m by March 2028 while existing borrowing amortises to £136.8m, opening a £64.3m gap inside two years.

officer.body:
Hi Liz,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the outturn report that went to Audit & Governance on 16 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. We hold 16 PWLB loans for Winchester totalling £159,010,462 against the £159.3m in your Table 3. Your Table 1 foots on every line — CFR of £280.8m is £68.3m General Fund plus £212.5m HRA; less £2.7m of other debt liabilities gives the £278.1m loans CFR; less £159.3m of borrowing gives the £118.8m of internal borrowing you state; and less £136.1m of balance sheet resources gives net investments of £17.3m. Your liability benchmark rebuilds exactly for every year too.

That benchmark is the reason we wrote. It reaches £201.1m by March 2028 while existing borrowing amortises to £136.8m — a £64.3m gap opening inside two years, and your paragraph 20.4 says exactly that. Since all £159.3m of your current debt is HRA and sits at 3.06%, the replacement question is a specific one rather than a general one, and it will be answered at whatever the HRA rate is on the day. That rate is gilt plus 40 basis points, sixty below the standard rate, and this afternoon on notice 314/26 five-year certainty closed at 5.34% and ten-year at 5.83%. July's sector lending was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — thin, and worth knowing before you are the one bringing a requirement to it.

The second thing is Table 5, which is the most striking benchmarking table we have read. Your bail-in exposure is 100% against 58% for similar authorities and 64% for all, and the weighted average maturity of the internally managed portfolio is one day against 45 days for peers. That is the most liquid and most bail-in-exposed portfolio we have priced anywhere.

Your paragraphs 17.8 and 17.10 explain it properly — short-term unsecured deposits and money market funds held for liquidity, with the MMFs bail-in 'light' in Arlingclose's assessment, and a snapshot that happened to catch a higher proportion in unsecured deposits. We are not suggesting anything is wrong; on a £16.6m year-end balance the absolute exposure is small. But the combination is unusual enough to be worth a sentence to members before someone else notices the 100%, and it is the sort of comparison that only shows up when you can see the whole sector at once.

Worth saying that your arrangement with Hampshire's Investments and Borrowing Team is the only shared treasury service we have come across in everything we have read this year, and paragraph 21.1 defends it well. Splitting day-to-day cash management from long-term borrowing decisions, and keeping the latter in-house, looks like the right line to draw — the borrowing decisions are the ones the £64.3m gap turns on.

On pricing: your PWLB book sits about £28.6m below par on the DMO's premature repayment curve today, 14 of the 16 loans. Standard caveats and we mean them — we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, four fit Winchester. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice is the one, given where Table 7 goes. HRA treasury & self-financing, since every pound you owe is HRA including the 2012 settlement. Counterparty concentration risk for the Table 5 point. And PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
